sentences.text: The Fairwork Cloudwork Ratings are a rating programme, a league table scoring cloudwork platforms against the five Fairwork Cloudwork Principles, each platform scored out of 10 on ten thresholds, two per principle (Labor Vector record); the 2025 ratings, in their authors' words, assess and score "basic standards of fairness in working arrangements on 16 cloudwork digital labour platforms" on fair pay, conditions, contracts, management and representation (the 2025 report).

The Labor Vector census asks of every resource "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains — and what kind of evidence does this resource bring to that question?" and places this one on four of its five intersections, labor producing AI, gains and losses, worker power and AI governing labor, with two kinds of evidence, rating against standards and worker testimony (Labor Vector record).

The project behind the ratings "studies working conditions on digital labour platforms and rates individual platforms based on their fairness to workers", its goal to show that "better and fairer platform jobs are possible" (the 2025 report); the trade press gives the 2025 edition as an assessment of 16 widely used platforms on five core principles (The Global Recruiter), and a Fairwork video asks "How fair are freelance and remote work platforms?" (YouTube, title only).

Cloudwork, in the report's definition, is work "that can be performed remotely through a digital labour platform", set against location-specific "geographically tethered work" (the 2025 report); it runs from microwork such as data labelling and processing, AI training and image categorisation to freelance services such as translation, web development or design (the 2025 report; the home page), and the census takes it as the labour object, naming the AI data work the report finds done for leading AI companies (Labor Vector record).

Cloudworkers are "generally classified as self-employed or independent workers on paid piece rates" (the 2025 report), whom the census records as supplying the labour, while the platforms rated and the requesters or clients who post work on them direct it (Labor Vector record).

A growing sector of cloudwork is "data services for artificial intelligence development in international supply chains", its clients among the world's leading AI companies, "such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Nvidia" (the 2025 report); the trade press calls many cloudwork tasks "fundamental for developing AI systems" (The Global Recruiter), and Fairwork AI states: "There is nothing “artificial” about the immense amount of human labour that builds, supports, and maintains AI systems" (Fairwork AI).

Of the workers of this class the archive holds that content moderators "perform semantic labor in its most brutal form: sorting meaning under conditions designed to be invisible", meaning being produced "by bodies, at metabolic cost" (#18), and that the labour of content moderators and of "the data labelers performing RLHF" is extracted, its non-compensation borne materially (#623).

The archive calls this ghost work "ground-truth labor", "the labor of telling the model what is already known to be true", distinct from variance-generative labor, and holds that ghost work scales and "is paid badly" (#163).

It counts annotators among the sources of semantic labor whose concealment is "the first marker of extraction" (#533), finds the literature of hidden AI labour stopping "at task-labor — annotation, moderation, the edge-case fix", naming the erased worker but not "that the erased thing is the provenance of meaning" (#144), and derives the semantic proletariat through moderators and annotators while holding that it is not "AI annotators" or "gig workers" (#1545).

The ratings rest on desk research, worker interviews and surveys, and interviews with platform management (the 2025 report); where managers do not engage, scoring is limited to desk research and worker surveys, and final scores are decided collectively by the core team and peer-reviewed (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record), platforms being given a chance to respond and earning points "only if they meet the criteria for each principle" (the home page), with the report, a platform search tool and the Principles and methodology pages as the data (Labor Vector record).

The survey of what the report calls "this third report" was collected between February 2024 and January 2025 and left responses from 776 workers in 100 countries (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record).

The governing limit is the authors': "Failing to achieve a point does not necessarily mean that a platform does not comply with the principle in question; it simply means that the research team did not find any evidence and/or they were unable to prove its compliance" (the 2025 report), which the census carries as a stated limit and as the negative tag "NOT a finding of non-compliance where a point is missing" (Labor Vector record); and the surveys "do not aim to build a representative set of experiences" but seek to understand how work is carried out and managed (the 2025 report), "NOT a representative survey of cloudworkers" in the census's tag (Labor Vector record).

In 2025 ComeUp, Elharefa and Translated scored 8, Creative Words and Terawork 7, Prolific 5, SoyFreelancer 4 and Appen 3, and the remaining eight no more than 2, three of them with no point evidenced (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record), Upwork at 1 and Amazon Mechanical Turk, Freelancer and Microworkers at 0 (the 2025 report's league table), and the census sets Turkopticon beside the record as its neighbour (Labor Vector record).

No platform reached 10, which only Creative Words has ever done, once, in 2023 (the 2025 report); the executive summary counts "the remaining nine platforms" where the key findings and the table give eight, an inconsistency the census records (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record), and the operator's cloudwork page lists the 2025 scores without Creative Words, Terawork its one platform at 7 (Fairwork cloudwork page).

Seven platforms evidenced systems to pay workers on time for all completed work, and four, ComeUp, Translated, Elharefa and Terawork, met the threshold "that the majority of workers should earn at least the local minimum wage" (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record), four of 16 "after costs" in the trade press's account (The Global Recruiter).

Nine platforms met the threshold on measures against unreasonable competition, overwork and unpaid labour, and for most no evidence was found that their terms are free of waivers of the right to legal recourse (the 2025 report); over half, the trade press reports, carry clauses such as "vague job descriptions, blanket liability clauses" (The Global Recruiter).

Six platforms received the point for recognising and engaging collective workers' bodies and none the second, collective governance or bargaining (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record); six "now formally recognise the right to organise – up from just 2 last year", none actively bargaining, and seven of 16 guard against risks "such as burnout or back pain" (The Global Recruiter), where the principle asks platforms to "be prepared to cooperate and negotiate" with workers' collective bodies (the home page).

The census finds no intersection with Labor Vector's instruments stated by the resource and reads the ratings as scoring "the intermediary that directs cloudwork (allocation, rejection, deactivation, contract terms)", thresholds 1.1 and 2.1 standing as "the report's own measures of unpaid labor" in its terms (Labor Vector record).

The authors attribute the growth in platforms acknowledging freedom of association to "Fairwork’s engagement" and count a record 56 changes by eight platforms, estimated to affect over two million workers (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record), made "Through direct engagement" in the trade press's account (The Global Recruiter), as the 2023 text on the operator's page found platforms incorporating fairness "as a result of engagement with Fairwork researchers" (Fairwork cloudwork page).

Of the surveyed workers 31.2% reported non-payment and 38% late payment, Global South workers report "discrimination and distrust when competing with workers from other regions" (the 2025 report), a line the Capture Registry finds in the report (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), and of 448 respondents 33.3% put the local minimum wage first and 18.3% payment for all completed work (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record).

The report finds platforms' own governance initiatives "insufficient in most cases to ensure basic compensation rights", cites platform work studies on how "algorithmic management accentuates opacity in decisions affecting workers" (the 2025 report), and its co-lead holds that voluntary improvements "will never be enough" (Valente, in The Global Recruiter).

On the census's reading the ratings answer whether a named platform shows evidence of meeting each threshold, which policies changed in the scoring dialogue and which rights surveyed workers rank highest, and do not answer the market-wide share below minimum wage, whether a platform with no point violates the principle, or the conditions of AI data work at outsourcing companies outside the platforms rated (Labor Vector record).

Who gains is "not recorded as a quantity" (Labor Vector record); in the census's worked questions the entity holds pay and conditions against minimum standards and platforms rated with a survey of 776 cloudworkers, while no record measures how gains divide among workers, employers, platforms and model providers, or how much of a system's training data any reported work produced (Labor Vector record).

The project is based at the Oxford Internet Institute and the WZB Berlin Social Science Center and financed by, among others, the BMZ, commissioned by GIZ, its five principles developed in 2018 at a multi-stakeholder workshop at the ILO and its cloudwork principles in 2020 (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record); the WZB calls Fairwork its joint project with the Oxford Internet Institute (WZB), and the certification site calls it "A non-profit spun out of the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) & Berlin Social Science Center (WZB)" (fair.work).

Of the earlier editions, the WZB reported the 2022 ratings, 15 platforms with the top score seven of ten (WZB), King's College London's portal holds that report, 34 pages, as "Work in the Plenatary Labour Market" (King's College London; its abstract), the operator's page carries 2025, 2023, 2022 and 2021 and still shows the 2023 text of 15 platforms (Fairwork cloudwork page), and Fairwork recorded the 2023 launch (YouTube, title only); the census gives the 2025 report as the third cloudwork report, with earlier reports in 2021 and 2023 (Labor Vector record), and the report calls itself both "this third report" and "this second cloudwork league table" (the 2025 report).

Beside the ratings Fairwork runs strands the census keeps apart: national location-based rankings in 38 countries and principles for the fair use of AI in the workplace (the home page; Labor Vector record), and a certification of the firms that commission AI data work, "based on evidence including the voices of the workers themselves" (fair.work), announced in the report to AI lead firms (the 2025 report), whose Fair Pay principle asks for "the local living wage after work-related costs" (fair.work).

The authors declare no connection with any platform and no conflict of interest and note sections in common with other Fairwork reports, and Scale/Remotasks, in its comment, holds the evaluation "overly subjective in key areas" (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record).

At the name the Capture Registry finds the programme held, its principles, scale, 16 platforms and operator the record's, reads "spun out of" as the composition's word for an operator the record gives as based at both, and gives the innocent reading first: the Overview gives the ratings' publisher, principles, scale and general findings and offers a platform's score (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

It finds the scores absent, "A rating programme is composed by its principles and its general verdict, without its ratings", the composition keeping "the standard" and dropping "the platforms it was applied to", the improvement given "without its cause", neither caveat reaching it, what the ratings are for left out, and one card, fair.work, drawn from another strand (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

The record landed on laborvector.org the same day and no card cites it (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); the census leaves unchecked the Principles and methodology pages, the search tool, the AI Principles and the earlier reports (Labor Vector record), and Wikipedia has no article on the ratings or on Fairwork (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

L_BA.text: The Fairwork Cloudwork Ratings are a rating programme, a league table scoring cloudwork platforms against the five Fairwork Cloudwork Principles, each platform scored out of 10 on ten thresholds, two per principle (Labor Vector record); the 2025 ratings, in their authors' words, assess and score "basic standards of fairness in working arrangements on 16 cloudwork digital labour platforms" on fair pay, conditions, contracts, management and representation (the 2025 report). The Labor Vector census asks of every resource "Who supplies the labor, who directs it, and who receives its gains — and what kind of evidence does this resource bring to that question?" and places this one on four of its five intersections, labor producing AI, gains and losses, worker power and AI governing labor, with two kinds of evidence, rating against standards and worker testimony (Labor Vector record). The project behind the ratings "studies working conditions on digital labour platforms and rates individual platforms based on their fairness to workers", its goal to show that "better and fairer platform jobs are possible" (the 2025 report); the trade press gives the 2025 edition as an assessment of 16 widely used platforms on five core principles (The Global Recruiter), and a Fairwork video asks "How fair are freelance and remote work platforms?" (YouTube, title only). Cloudwork, in the report's definition, is work "that can be performed remotely through a digital labour platform", set against location-specific "geographically tethered work" (the 2025 report); it runs from microwork such as data labelling and processing, AI training and image categorisation to freelance services such as translation, web development or design (the 2025 report; the home page), and the census takes it as the labour object, naming the AI data work the report finds done for leading AI companies (Labor Vector record). Cloudworkers are "generally classified as self-employed or independent workers on paid piece rates" (the 2025 report), whom the census records as supplying the labour, while the platforms rated and the requesters or clients who post work on them direct it (Labor Vector record). A growing sector of cloudwork is "data services for artificial intelligence development in international supply chains", its clients among the world's leading AI companies, "such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Nvidia" (the 2025 report); the trade press calls many cloudwork tasks "fundamental for developing AI systems" (The Global Recruiter), and Fairwork AI states: "There is nothing “artificial” about the immense amount of human labour that builds, supports, and maintains AI systems" (Fairwork AI). Of the workers of this class the archive holds that content moderators "perform semantic labor in its most brutal form: sorting meaning under conditions designed to be invisible", meaning being produced "by bodies, at metabolic cost" (#18), and that the labour of content moderators and of "the data labelers performing RLHF" is extracted, its non-compensation borne materially (#623). The archive calls this ghost work "ground-truth labor", "the labor of telling the model what is already known to be true", distinct from variance-generative labor, and holds that ghost work scales and "is paid badly" (#163). It counts annotators among the sources of semantic labor whose concealment is "the first marker of extraction" (#533), finds the literature of hidden AI labour stopping "at task-labor — annotation, moderation, the edge-case fix", naming the erased worker but not "that the erased thing is the provenance of meaning" (#144), and derives the semantic proletariat through moderators and annotators while holding that it is not "AI annotators" or "gig workers" (#1545). The ratings rest on desk research, worker interviews and surveys, and interviews with platform management (the 2025 report); where managers do not engage, scoring is limited to desk research and worker surveys, and final scores are decided collectively by the core team and peer-reviewed (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record), platforms being given a chance to respond and earning points "only if they meet the criteria for each principle" (the home page), with the report, a platform search tool and the Principles and methodology pages as the data (Labor Vector record). The survey of what the report calls "this third report" was collected between February 2024 and January 2025 and left responses from 776 workers in 100 countries (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record). The governing limit is the authors': "Failing to achieve a point does not necessarily mean that a platform does not comply with the principle in question; it simply means that the research team did not find any evidence and/or they were unable to prove its compliance" (the 2025 report), which the census carries as a stated limit and as the negative tag "NOT a finding of non-compliance where a point is missing" (Labor Vector record); and the surveys "do not aim to build a representative set of experiences" but seek to understand how work is carried out and managed (the 2025 report), "NOT a representative survey of cloudworkers" in the census's tag (Labor Vector record). In 2025 ComeUp, Elharefa and Translated scored 8, Creative Words and Terawork 7, Prolific 5, SoyFreelancer 4 and Appen 3, and the remaining eight no more than 2, three of them with no point evidenced (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record), Upwork at 1 and Amazon Mechanical Turk, Freelancer and Microworkers at 0 (the 2025 report's league table), and the census sets Turkopticon beside the record as its neighbour (Labor Vector record). No platform reached 10, which only Creative Words has ever done, once, in 2023 (the 2025 report); the executive summary counts "the remaining nine platforms" where the key findings and the table give eight, an inconsistency the census records (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record), and the operator's cloudwork page lists the 2025 scores without Creative Words, Terawork its one platform at 7 (Fairwork cloudwork page). Seven platforms evidenced systems to pay workers on time for all completed work, and four, ComeUp, Translated, Elharefa and Terawork, met the threshold "that the majority of workers should earn at least the local minimum wage" (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record), four of 16 "after costs" in the trade press's account (The Global Recruiter). Nine platforms met the threshold on measures against unreasonable competition, overwork and unpaid labour, and for most no evidence was found that their terms are free of waivers of the right to legal recourse (the 2025 report); over half, the trade press reports, carry clauses such as "vague job descriptions, blanket liability clauses" (The Global Recruiter). Six platforms received the point for recognising and engaging collective workers' bodies and none the second, collective governance or bargaining (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record); six "now formally recognise the right to organise – up from just 2 last year", none actively bargaining, and seven of 16 guard against risks "such as burnout or back pain" (The Global Recruiter), where the principle asks platforms to "be prepared to cooperate and negotiate" with workers' collective bodies (the home page). The census finds no intersection with Labor Vector's instruments stated by the resource and reads the ratings as scoring "the intermediary that directs cloudwork (allocation, rejection, deactivation, contract terms)", thresholds 1.1 and 2.1 standing as "the report's own measures of unpaid labor" in its terms (Labor Vector record). The authors attribute the growth in platforms acknowledging freedom of association to "Fairwork’s engagement" and count a record 56 changes by eight platforms, estimated to affect over two million workers (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record), made "Through direct engagement" in the trade press's account (The Global Recruiter), as the 2023 text on the operator's page found platforms incorporating fairness "as a result of engagement with Fairwork researchers" (Fairwork cloudwork page). Of the surveyed workers 31.2% reported non-payment and 38% late payment, Global South workers report "discrimination and distrust when competing with workers from other regions" (the 2025 report), a line the Capture Registry finds in the report (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), and of 448 respondents 33.3% put the local minimum wage first and 18.3% payment for all completed work (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record). The report finds platforms' own governance initiatives "insufficient in most cases to ensure basic compensation rights", cites platform work studies on how "algorithmic management accentuates opacity in decisions affecting workers" (the 2025 report), and its co-lead holds that voluntary improvements "will never be enough" (Valente, in The Global Recruiter). On the census's reading the ratings answer whether a named platform shows evidence of meeting each threshold, which policies changed in the scoring dialogue and which rights surveyed workers rank highest, and do not answer the market-wide share below minimum wage, whether a platform with no point violates the principle, or the conditions of AI data work at outsourcing companies outside the platforms rated (Labor Vector record). Who gains is "not recorded as a quantity" (Labor Vector record); in the census's worked questions the entity holds pay and conditions against minimum standards and platforms rated with a survey of 776 cloudworkers, while no record measures how gains divide among workers, employers, platforms and model providers, or how much of a system's training data any reported work produced (Labor Vector record). The project is based at the Oxford Internet Institute and the WZB Berlin Social Science Center and financed by, among others, the BMZ, commissioned by GIZ, its five principles developed in 2018 at a multi-stakeholder workshop at the ILO and its cloudwork principles in 2020 (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record); the WZB calls Fairwork its joint project with the Oxford Internet Institute (WZB), and the certification site calls it "A non-profit spun out of the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) & Berlin Social Science Center (WZB)" (fair.work). Of the earlier editions, the WZB reported the 2022 ratings, 15 platforms with the top score seven of ten (WZB), King's College London's portal holds that report, 34 pages, as "Work in the Plenatary Labour Market" (King's College London; its abstract), the operator's page carries 2025, 2023, 2022 and 2021 and still shows the 2023 text of 15 platforms (Fairwork cloudwork page), and Fairwork recorded the 2023 launch (YouTube, title only); the census gives the 2025 report as the third cloudwork report, with earlier reports in 2021 and 2023 (Labor Vector record), and the report calls itself both "this third report" and "this second cloudwork league table" (the 2025 report). Beside the ratings Fairwork runs strands the census keeps apart: national location-based rankings in 38 countries and principles for the fair use of AI in the workplace (the home page; Labor Vector record), and a certification of the firms that commission AI data work, "based on evidence including the voices of the workers themselves" (fair.work), announced in the report to AI lead firms (the 2025 report), whose Fair Pay principle asks for "the local living wage after work-related costs" (fair.work). The authors declare no connection with any platform and no conflict of interest and note sections in common with other Fairwork reports, and Scale/Remotasks, in its comment, holds the evaluation "overly subjective in key areas" (the 2025 report; Labor Vector record). At the name the Capture Registry finds the programme held, its principles, scale, 16 platforms and operator the record's, reads "spun out of" as the composition's word for an operator the record gives as based at both, and gives the innocent reading first: the Overview gives the ratings' publisher, principles, scale and general findings and offers a platform's score (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). It finds the scores absent, "A rating programme is composed by its principles and its general verdict, without its ratings", the composition keeping "the standard" and dropping "the platforms it was applied to", the improvement given "without its cause", neither caveat reaching it, what the ratings are for left out, and one card, fair.work, drawn from another strand (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). The record landed on laborvector.org the same day and no card cites it (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); the census leaves unchecked the Principles and methodology pages, the search tool, the AI Principles and the earlier reports (Labor Vector record), and Wikipedia has no article on the ratings or on Fairwork (Wikipedia, 2026-10-29).

delta.T_vs_LB: At 'Fairwork Cloudwork Ratings' (T1, eight cards: B1–B8, B5 and B7 videos unreachable, titles only; 244 words) the composition gives the programme by its publisher and its five principles. Composed from its cards: the definition at the report's and the trade press's grain (B1 F1, B6 F47: an evaluation of cloudwork platforms against five principles; B1 F2 'rates individual platforms'), cloudwork as online remote platform work (B1 F24), the 2025 assessment of 16 platforms (B1 F1; B6 F47), the operator as 'spun out of the Oxford Internet Institute and the Berlin Social Science Center WZB' (B8 F55, the certification site's own words, 'A non-profit spun out of the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) & Berlin Social Science Center (WZB)', with B1 F32's 'based at' coarsened), the general verdict (B4 F43, the 2023 text: 'most cloudwork platforms are not meeting minimum standards'), the 'formal recognition of the right to organize' (B6 F51, six up from two; B1 F12), the Global South (B1 F22: 'discrimination and distrust'). Substituted reading: the principles are composed with the trade press's findings about platforms as their content. B6 reports that only four of 16 show the local minimum wage 'after costs' (F49), that over half carry 'vague job descriptions, blanket liability clauses' (F50), that only seven guard against 'burnout or back pain' (F51); T composes Fair Pay as a wage 'proportional to local or national minimum standards after costs', Fair Conditions as protection from 'burnout, back pain', Fair Contracts as terms 'without blanket liability clauses or vague job descriptions'. Findings of absence become definitions of the standard. Limit dropped: the authors' governing limit, that a missing point is not a finding of non-compliance (B1 F18), and the survey limit (B1 F19): neither is composed, and 'struggle to meet basic fairness standards' stands at the force of the 2023 page (F43) and the trade press without them (the capture finds the same: CAP-1-06). Available, not composed: the scores themselves (B1 F4, F6, F7; B4 F42), the threshold counts (F8, F9, F10), the second representation point awarded to none (F12, in part), the 56 changes and their cause (F13, F14, F52, F44; CAP-1-05: 'without its cause'), no platform at 10 (F31), the survey and its findings (F20, F21, F23), the method (F15–F17), AI data work and its clients (B1 F27, F28; B6 F48): T names no AI at all, though the report's title names 'AI Supply Chain Governance' and card 8 is Fairwork's certification of 'the human labour behind AI' (F54), from which T takes only the operator's origin; the goal (F3; the registry's PER reading: purpose absent, CAP-1-12); piece rates (F26); the editions (B2, B3, B4, B5: F38, F40, F41, F45, F64). Outside the cards: 'digital hazards'; 'grievance channels'; 'lower effective compensation relative to local costs of living' and 'higher rates of unaddressed discrimination' (no field source gives a rate; force raised against F22's 'discrimination and distrust'). T1-8's 'based on concrete evidence provided for each threshold' stands at the grain of B1's scoring rule ('Points are only awarded if clear evidence exists for each threshold examined'), a sentence of the report not ledgered as a claim. Composed without attribution: everything, at the coarse grain of a programme description (recorded, not a breach), except the principles' wording, composed at the trade press's resolution from its findings (recorded as substituted reading). Content replaced by use: the pointer to 'platform scorecards' (T1-11) and the closer offering 'a specific platform's score' (T1-12), the scores the body does not give (CAP-1-04).

E_F.type: C (public entity: a rating programme and its reports)
E_F.definition: the ratings of the Fairwork project, based at the Oxford Internet Institute, University of Oxford, and the WZB Berlin Social Science Center and financed among others by the BMZ, commissioned by GIZ, that assess and score basic standards of fairness on cloudwork digital labour platforms (work performed remotely through a platform, from microwork such as data labelling and AI training to freelance work; workers generally self-employed on piece rates) against the five Fairwork Cloudwork Principles, fair pay, conditions, contracts, management and representation, each platform out of 10 on ten thresholds, by desk research, platform manager evidence and worker surveys, a point awarded only on evidence; the 2025 report (16 platforms; 776 workers in 100 countries): three platforms at 8, two at 7, eight at 2 or less, Amazon Mechanical Turk, Freelancer and Microworkers at 0, four meeting the minimum wage, none the bargaining point, 56 changes through Fairwork's engagement; its stated limits that a missing point is not a finding of non-compliance and that the survey is not representative; AI data work for leading AI companies a growing sector of the work rated; earlier editions 2021, 2022, 2023; beside it the location-based ratings, the workplace AI principles and a certification of the firms that commission AI data work (fair.work, 'a non-profit spun out of' the OII and the WZB); no Wikipedia article

E_A.definition: the same ratings, in the Labor Vector census record and the archive's deposits: a rating programme scoring cloudwork platforms against the five principles, placed on four intersections of the census's question (labour producing AI, gains and losses, worker power, AI governing labour), whose evidence (rating against standards, worker testimony) records who supplies the labour (cloudworkers on piece rates) and who directs it (the platforms and the requesters) and does not record who gains as a quantity; read by the archive as scoring the intermediary that directs cloudwork, its thresholds on payment for all completed work and paid loading time the report's own measures of unpaid labour; answering whether a named platform evidences each threshold and not whether a platform with no point violates it; whose AI data workers perform semantic labor at bodily cost (#18), have their labour extracted (#623), are ground-truth labourers, scaled and badly paid (#163), bearing-cost sources whose concealment marks extraction (#533), named by a literature that stops short of the provenance of meaning (#144), and pass through semantic labour toward, without being, the semantic proletariat (#1545); composed at its name by its principles and verdict without its ratings (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29)
